scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Kachchhi Ghodi dance originated in the Shekhawati region of Rajasthan, India.
It is traditionally associated with and performed by members of the Kamdholi, Sarghara, Bhambi, and Bhavi communities.
Over time, its popularity spread beyond Rajasthan, becoming an adopted folk tradition in other Indian states, including Maharashtra and Gujarat.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Kachchhi Ghodi is commonly performed during wedding ceremonies to welcome and entertain the bridegroom's party, as well as during diverse social settings and cultural events.
For some dancers, performing the art form serves as a professional livelihood.
The narrative aspects celebrate local heroism and traditional folklore.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Performers step inside a novelty horse frame secured around the waist and move across the performance space.
In group formations, dancers stand on opposite sides holding swords and run back and forth quickly.
When viewed from above, this rapid back-and-forth movement creates the visual illusion of flowers opening and closing.
Watch for Opening flower formation.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The dance is performed to the accompaniment of musicians playing the dhol (drum) and flute.
A live singer narrates folk tales of mock fights, focusing on the exploits of local bandits such as Bhanwariya, considered the Rajasthani equivalent of Robin Hood.
Listen for the dhol, flute, ghungroo.
A dynamic combination of deep dhol drumbeats, melodic flute lines, percussive ankle-bell jingles, and loud narrative singing describing mock sword fights and legendary bandits.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dancers wear a traditional kurta and turban.
The novelty horse costume features a papier-mâché shell built over a bamboo frame, embellished with brightly colored fabric and Shisha (mirror-work embroidery).
The dummy horse does not have legs; instead, fabric drapes from the dancer's waist to cover the legs entirely.

wardrobe.from_sources: Dancers wear a traditional kurta and turban. The novelty horse costume features a papier-mâché shell built over a bamboo frame, embellished with brightly colored fabric and Shisha (mirror-work embroidery). The dummy horse does not have legs; instead, fabric drapes from the dancer's waist to cover the legs entirely. Ghungroo bells are tied around the ankles. It is typically performed in open settings, streets during wedding processions, or stage shows.
